Since the program began in 2019, more than 3,000 trees have been adopted by individuals, families, and local businesses. How It Works • Choose a tree from the online map and submit an adoption form. Each participant may adopt up to two trees. • Water your tree at least once a week from May through September. The city will provide a free 15-gallon watering bag upon registration. • Report any damage, pests, or signs of disease through the city's app. Do not prune branches yourself; trained city staff will handle all trimming. Benefits Adopters may name their tree, and a small tag with the chosen name will be attached to it. Those who complete a full season of care will receive a certificate of appreciation. Registration opens on April 1 and closes when all available trees have been adopted. Participation is free of charge.

Its aim is to close the digital gap between generations and regions. Our Services — Learning Programs: We offer free in-person classes at community centers, as well as online courses that learners can take at any time that suits them. — Device Support: Residents aged 65 and older can borrow tablets for up to three months at no cost. — Online Safety: We provide guidance on recognizing phishing messages and protecting personal information on the Internet. — Volunteer Network: University students who complete our 20-hour training course can serve as digital mentors in their local communities.

For a long time, sleep was regarded as a passive state in which the brain simply rests. Recent research, however, shows that the sleeping brain is remarkably active, especially when it comes to memory. ① <u>During deep sleep, the hippocampus replays the experiences of the day and transfers important information to the cortex for long-term storage.</u> ② <u>Since sleep is merely a period of mental inactivity, cutting it short has little effect on how well we remember what we have learned.</u> ③ <u>In one study, students who slept after memorizing a list of words recalled significantly more of them the next morning than those who stayed awake.</u> ④ <u>Sleep also appears to help the brain discard trivial details, making room for new learning.</u> These findings suggest that a good night's sleep is not a luxury but an essential part of effective learning.

Many drivers today rely on GPS navigation even to reach places they have visited dozens of times. ( ① ) The technology is undeniably helpful: it calculates the fastest route, warns of traffic jams, and spares us the stress of getting lost. ( ② ) Researchers have found that people who follow turn-by-turn directions form far weaker mental maps of the areas they travel through than those who find their own way. ( ③ ) In one study, participants who used a navigation app to walk through an unfamiliar neighborhood later struggled to sketch the route or to point toward landmarks they had passed. ( ④ ) Some scientists therefore suggest occasionally switching the device off, even on familiar trips, to keep these navigational skills from fading.

Many people assume that those who procrastinate are simply lazy or bad at planning. They buy new calendars, download productivity apps, and promise themselves they will start earlier next time. Yet research suggests that putting things off is less a problem of time management than a problem of <u>                    </u>. When a task makes us feel bored, anxious, or insecure about our abilities, avoiding it offers immediate relief. Scrolling through social media or cleaning the kitchen temporarily lifts our mood, even though we know the task is still waiting. The trouble is that this relief is short-lived. As the deadline approaches, the original bad feelings return, now joined by guilt and stress, which makes the task even more unpleasant to face. This explains why simply making a better schedule rarely works. A more effective approach is to notice the uncomfortable feelings a task stirs up and to respond to them with curiosity rather than self-criticism. Being kind to ourselves about past delays, it turns out, makes us less likely to delay again.

When a plant or animal is introduced to a new region, it often leaves behind the predators, parasites, and diseases that kept its population in check in its native range. Ecologists call this the “enemy release hypothesis.” Freed from these natural enemies, the newcomer can devote more energy to growth and reproduction rather than to defense, allowing it to outcompete native species that are still burdened by their own local enemies. Purple loosestrife, a wetland plant from Europe, is a well-known example. It spread aggressively across North American marshes, where few insects fed on it, and crowded out many native plants. Its expansion slowed in many areas only after scientists deliberately released several European beetles that specialize in eating the plant. This strategy, known as biological control, essentially reunites an invader with one of its old enemies. Even so, it must be applied with great care, since an imported control agent could itself become a problem if it begins to attack native species.

When a powerful storm surge rolls toward a tropical coastline, what stands between the sea and the villages behind it is often not a concrete wall but a tangle of roots. Mangrove forests, which grow in the salty shallows where land meets ocean, slow incoming waves with their dense, arching root systems, considerably reducing wave height before the water reaches the shore. Their roots also trap sediment carried by the tides, gradually building up the land and helping coastlines keep pace with rising seas. Unlike seawalls, which crack, require costly repairs, and can even worsen erosion on neighboring shores, mangroves repair themselves and grow stronger over time. Yet in many regions, they have been cleared to make room for shrimp farms and tourist resorts, leaving coastal communities exposed. Protecting and replanting these forests may be one of the most cost-effective defenses that coastal nations have.

We tend to treat forgetting as a failure of memory, something to be fought with supplements and brain-training apps. Yet a growing number of neuroscientists argue that ______________________________. Our brains are constantly bombarded with information, and most of it is trivial. If we remembered every detail of every day, such as where we parked the car each morning for the last ten years or every face glimpsed on a crowded train, we would struggle to retrieve what actually matters. By actively weakening connections that are rarely used, the brain clears away outdated details, such as an old phone number, so that new and relevant ones can be stored and accessed more easily. Forgetting also allows us to generalize: by losing specific particulars, we are able to extract the broader patterns that guide our future decisions. In this sense, a mind that forgets well is not a weaker mind but a more efficient one.

다음 글의 (A)에 들어갈 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은? To the Residents of Greenfield (A) Do you find it difficult to book train tickets online or make a video call with your grandchildren? You are not alone. As more and more everyday services move to the internet, many older residents feel left behind. To help them keep up with these changes, the Greenfield City Council is launching a new program this spring. Starting April 7, residents aged 65 and over can attend weekly classes at any of the city's five public libraries. Trained instructors will teach participants how to use smartphones and tablets, send emails, access online banking safely, and recognize common internet scams. Classes are kept small, with no more than eight learners per group, so that everyone receives personal attention. Devices will be provided for those who do not have their own. All classes are free of charge. Seats are limited, so please register in advance by calling 555-0123 or visiting the front desk of your local library. Take the first step toward a more connected life!
